entries.text: Skip to content Research / Alternative Fuels & Nanoparticles 05 / Sustainable Energy · Experimental Research Alternative Fuels & Nanoparticles Fuel preparation, characterization, and engine testing across biodiesel, plastic-derived fuels, and nanoparticle-containing blends. My work connects the composition and properties of alternative fuels with their performance, combustion behaviour, and exhaust response. The research includes laboratory fuel preparation, comparative engine measurements, and analysis of experimental results. 01 Biodiesel Preparation from plant oils, animal fat, and waste cooking oil, followed by fuel-property evaluation and blend studies. → 02 Plastic-Derived Fuels Waste-plastic pyrolysis, liquid recovery, filtration, and fractional distillation, with original laboratory photographs. → 03 Combustion & Emissions Research-engine instrumentation, combustion analysis, fuel consumption, exhaust-gas measurements, and smoke-opacity testing. → 04 Nanoparticle Fuel Additives Studies of ZnO and CuO additives in alternative-fuel blends, with links to the associated peer-reviewed publications. → Alternative fuel research topics Experimental Scope From Fuel Properties to Engine Response Fuel composition, blend fraction, engine loading, and measurement conditions provide the basis for comparing each fuel with its reference. The measurements available differ between projects. Fuel Characterization Density, viscosity, calorific value, flash and pour points, and chemical characterization where available. Performance & Combustion Power, thermal efficiency, specific fuel consumption, cylinder-pressure response, and heat-release analysis. Exhaust Measurements Smoke opacity and gas-specific emissions are interpreted according to the instruments and scope of the individual study. Project Records Reports, Publications & Funded Research Explore the 2019 undergraduate project, the AEPC and UGC research records, and the institutionally supported hybrid-biodiesel work. The grants section includes the complete abstracts from the reports. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Alternative Fuels / Biodiesel SUSTAINABLE ENERGY / BIODIESEL Biodiesel from Diverse Oils and Fats I have prepared biodiesel from Jatropha seed oil, castor oil, palm oil, animal fat, soybean oil, sunflower oil, and waste cooking oil. My work explores the use of plant-based, animal-derived, and waste-derived feedstocks for alternative fuel preparation. Overview Biodiesel Plastic Fuel Combustion and Emission Nanoparticles Alternative fuels research Feedstocks Used in My Work The choice of oil or fat is an important part of biodiesel preparation. Feedstocks differ in composition, moisture, and free fatty acid content, which can influence pretreatment needs, conversion, and final fuel properties. Jatropha seed oil Castor oil Palm oil Animal fat Soybean oil Sunflower oil Waste cooking oil Understanding Biodiesel Preparation Biodiesel consists of fatty acid alkyl esters, commonly produced by reacting oils or fats with an alcohol through transesterification. The following stages outline the general preparation process; the treatment required depends on the feedstock. 01 / PREPARATION Feedstock Preparation Oils and fats are prepared for conversion. Filtration removes suspended material, while moisture and acidity help determine whether further pretreatment is needed. 02 / CONVERSION Reaction and Mixing During transesterification, triglycerides react with an alcohol to form biodiesel and glycerol. Mixing and temperature control are important aspects of the process. 03 / RECOVERY Separation and Purification After reaction, product phases are separated. Further purification and drying help prepare the biodiesel for fuel-property evaluation. Inside the Laboratory Photographs from feedstock handling and biodiesel preparation. Select an image to view the original. Two beakers containing brown liquid on laboratory heating and stirring equipment View original laboratory preparation photograph 01 / LABORATORY PREPARATION Heating and Mixing Setup Beakers and laboratory heating equipment used during biodiesel preparation, with a probe positioned in one vessel for monitoring. Waste cooking oil in a container lined with white filter cloth View original waste cooking oil filtration photograph 02 / FEEDSTOCK HANDLING Waste Cooking Oil Filtration Cloth filtration of waste cooking oil helps remove suspended food particles and other solid material before further processing. A researcher beside separating funnels containing visibly distinct liquid layers View original biodiesel production photograph 03 / PRODUCT SEPARATION Biodiesel Preparation and Separation A laboratory demonstration of phase separation using separating funnels. Distinct liquid layers are visible during product recovery. A handful of mottled oilseeds held in an open palm View original oilseed photograph 04 / FEEDSTOCK SOURCES Oilseed Feedstock Oilseeds photographed during feedstock-related work, illustrating the plant-derived starting materials considered in biodiesel preparation. From Preparation to Fuel Evaluation Preparing biodiesel is the first step towards understanding its suitability as an alternative fuel. Properties such as viscosity, density, acidity, and moisture content help characterise the product. Engine testing provides a separate assessment of performance, combustion, and exhaust emissions. entries.description: Explore laboratory work by Rupesh Lal Karn on engine combustion, exhaust emissions, smoke opacity, instrumentation, and experimental measurements.
entries.headings: Combustion and Emission Combustion Testing Emission and Opacity Testing Inside the Laboratory Research Engine Setup Reviewing Experimental Measurements Vehicle Testing and Instrument Checks Instrument readings and record keeping Connecting Combustion with Emissions
entries.text: Skip to content Research / Alternative Fuels / Combustion & Emissions SUSTAINABLE ENERGY / ENGINE RESEARCH Combustion and Emission Experimental work on engine combustion, exhaust emissions, and smoke opacity. These photographs document laboratory testing, engine instrumentation, and the review of experimental measurements. Overview Biodiesel Plastic Fuel Combustion and Emission Nanoparticles Alternative fuels research 01 / ENERGY CONVERSION Combustion Testing Combustion testing examines how fuel burns inside an engine and how chemical energy is converted into useful work. Cylinder pressure recorded against crank angle can be used to study combustion timing, pressure development, and heat-release behaviour. Engine speed, load, and fuel consumption provide additional context for comparing operating conditions and evaluating alternative fuel blends. 02 / EXHAUST CHARACTERISATION Emission and Opacity Testing Emission testing examines engine exhaust to understand the environmental effects of fuel use. Depending on the analyser, measurements may include carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen oxides. Smoke opacity testing measures how much light is blocked by an exhaust sample. It helps assess smoke behaviour and complements gas measurements; it is not a direct measurement of particulate mass. Understanding the tests Inside the Laboratory Engine testing, instrument checks, and experimental data review. Select a photograph to view the original image. Laboratory engine test rig with control instruments and a computer displaying engine analysis software View original research engine setup photo 01 / ENGINE TEST FACILITY Research Engine Setup The engine test rig, instrumentation panel, and computer interface used for laboratory investigations of engine performance and combustion. Researchers reviewing measurements on a computer beside an engine instrumentation panel View original combustion testing photo 02 / COMBUSTION ANALYSIS Reviewing Experimental Measurements Collaborative review of engine test measurements at the data-acquisition workstation, connecting instrument readings with the interpretation of combustion behaviour. A laboratory group working with test equipment beside a vehicle with its bonnet open View original emission testing photo 03 / EMISSION TESTING Vehicle Testing and Instrument Checks Preparation and inspection of testing equipment during a vehicle laboratory session. Instrument checks and consistent operating conditions support meaningful exhaust measurements. Two researchers checking a handheld instrument and recording observations beside an engine test rig View original opacity testing photo 04 / SMOKE OPACITY Instrument readings and record keeping Checking instrument readings and recording observations during engine laboratory work associated with smoke opacity testing. Connecting Combustion with Emissions Combustion and exhaust measurements provide complementary views of engine operation. Examining them together helps assess the relationships between fuel properties, operating conditions, energy conversion, and pollutant formation. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Scientific data analysis Scientific Data Analysis I analyse measurements from functional materials, crystal and magnetic studies, thermal experiments, and electrochemistry. MATLAB-supported processing, quantitative feature extraction, physical calculations, and statistical assessment connect measured signals with interpretable material descriptors and response parameters. Characterization Crystal & magnetic data Thermal & electrochemical Fit quality MATLAB workflow Engine analysis Research applications Page sections Materials Characterization Each measurement requires its own processing choices. Baseline treatment, fitting constraints, normalization, and feature selection are retained alongside the extracted quantities. Measurement Analysis Quantities interpreted XRD Baseline correction and selected diffraction-profile fitting Peak position, basal spacing, width, area, and apparent stacking coherence Raman Corresponding-feature identification and spectral-profile fitting Frequency shifts, linewidths, and selected relative spectral contributions FTIR Baseline treatment and integration over defined spectral windows Band areas, band-area fractions, and lattice-normalized ratios XPS Survey quantification and constrained high-resolution envelope analysis Elemental ratios and relative chemical-envelope contributions Gas sorption Interpretation of surface-area and pore-analysis outputs Gas-accessible area, pore volume, and operational pore descriptors Zeta potential / DLS Comparison of electrokinetic and hydrodynamic measurements Zeta-potential magnitude and operational dispersion size SEM / EDX Morphology review and comparison of elemental-analysis outputs Observed particle or layer features, elemental distributions, and reported composition Characterization analysis table; scroll horizontally on small screens Explore characterization-derived descriptors → Crystal and Magnetic-Material Data Structural and magnetic measurements are interpreted alongside composition, sample preparation, orientation, and measurement conditions. XRD & Rietveld refinement Phase identification, diffraction-profile comparison, and structural refinement support the interpretation of magnetic powders and crystalline materials. Magnetic measurements Comparisons retain field, temperature, sample orientation, and preparation history so that changes in measured response can be assessed in context. Magnetic-domain analysis Lorentz TEM analysis examines domain-related electron contrast and spatial magnetic features, retaining the imaging conditions used to interpret them. Single-crystal measurements My visiting research includes angle- and temperature-dependent dHvA measurements on HfSn₂ crystals. Sample orientation and measurement conditions remain part of the data context. Explore crystal growth and magnetic materials → Thermal and Electrochemical Analysis Thermal measurements Event selection and transient segmentation define which part of the measurement is being quantified. TGA / DTG: event boundaries, conversion, derivative peaks, and multi-rate comparison. Photothermal response: ambient correction, heating–cooling windows, amplitudes, time constants, and transient area. Reference calculations: keep directly measured quantities separate from calibrated or extrapolated estimates. TGA methods → Photothermal methods → Electrochemical measurements Potential, time, and frequency representations provide complementary views of the electrode response. CV: branch alignment, loop integration, background separation, and scan-rate comparisons. EIS: impedance components, phase, frequency-dependent capacitance, and consistency checks. GCD: charge–discharge segmentation, capacitance, charge balance, and energy integration. Electrochemical methods → Fit Quality and Physical Consistency A fitted curve is one part of the analysis. Residual behaviour, parameter identifiability, uncertainty, and sensitivity are examined in the relevant modelling tasks. Residual structure Look for systematic deviations and temporal dependence that summary fit measures can conceal. Parameter identifiability Examine whether available measurements can distinguish the fitted parameters. Sensitivity Assess the effects of fitting windows, processing choices, and descriptor definitions. Uncertainty Use parameter intervals and resampling in the analyses where they are applicable. Model comparison Consider complexity, information criteria, stability, and appropriate withheld observations. Physical consistency Check units, limiting cases, sign conventions, and the plausibility of calculated quantities. Analysis choices follow the measurement and research question. Fitted parameters are interpreted with their units, assumptions, sensitivity, and physical consistency. MATLAB Analysis Workflow Organize Preserve raw files, sample identity, units, experimental settings, and acquisition metadata. Process Apply measurement-specific correction, interpolation, segmentation, or filtering, documenting the choices. Quantify Extract features, calculate integrals, apply physical definitions, and assemble comparison tables. Assess Check residuals, uncertainty, sensitivity, parameter stability, and physical consistency. Visualize Use clear axes, consistent units, meaningful normalization, and comparable scales. Interpret Connect the observations to the research question while retaining assumptions and experimental limits. Earlier Engineering Analysis My earlier engineering research and publications include alternative fuels, biodiesel blends, plastic pyrolysis oil, nanoparticle-assisted fuels, and engine testing. Analysis connects fuel preparation and operating conditions with performance, combustion, emissions, and thermal accounting. Explore related publications → Performance analysis Fuel-consumption, power, and efficiency calculations support comparisons under defined load, speed, and fuel conditions. Combustion analysis Combustion measurements and derived quantities are interpreted using the applicable engine protocol, acquisition settings, and calculation assumptions. Emission analysis Exhaust measurements are compared with consistent units, operating conditions, and instrument context. Concentration measurements remain distinct from mass-specific emission factors. Thermal-balance accounting Fuel-energy input, useful output, measured heat-loss terms, and the balance remainder support energy-distribution analysis. BSFC = ṁf / Pb ηb = Pb / (ṁf × LHV) Representative engineering calculations Representative definitions: ṁf is fuel mass-flow rate, Pb is brake power, and LHV is lower heating value. Unit conversions and measurement conventions must be consistent. Research Applications Graduate materials research Characterization-derived descriptors, multi-rate thermal kinetics, photothermal transients, and electrochemical response models support my work on MXene-based materials. The modelling pages describe governing equations, assumptions, circuit structures, and numerical methods. Explore modelling methods → Published engineering research My publications address fuel properties, engine performance, thermal balances, combustion, and emissions across alternative-fuel systems. entries.title: Descriptor Extraction
entries.description: Explore characterization-derived descriptors from XRD, XPS, Raman, FTIR, BET, SEM/EDX, and zeta potential in Rupesh Lal Karn’s materials research.
entries.headings: Descriptor Extraction X-ray Diffraction XPS Raman Spectroscopy FTIR BET & Gas Sorption SEM / EDX Zeta Potential & DLS From Measurement to Model Input
entries.text: Skip to content Research / Modelling / Descriptor extraction Descriptor Extraction I extract interpretable variables from characterization measurements to describe material structure, surface chemistry, accessible interfaces, and dispersion. Baseline treatment, profile fitting, integration, and physical transformations connect each measured signal with a defined descriptor. The schematics below introduce the measurements and the meaning of the extracted quantities. XRD XPS Raman FTIR BET SEM / EDX Zeta Characterization methods XRD schematic showing peak position, full width at half maximum, integrated peak area, and layered crystal structure. Open XRD schematic XRD · Schematic Enlarge image Structural descriptors X-ray Diffraction Diffraction-profile modelling separates peak position, broadening, and area to characterize basal spacing and apparent stacking coherence. Basal spacing, d Interplanar distance obtained from Bragg’s law. Tracks spacing changes between corresponding reflections. Peak width, β Full width at half maximum. Describes broadening from coherence, strain, and instrumental contributions. Apparent Lc A Scherrer-type stacking-coherence estimate. Provides a comparative structural descriptor, rather than a direct flake-thickness measurement. Area / parent index Integrated intensity measures for selected regions. Track diffraction features without directly determining a residual-phase fraction. MATLAB: baseline correction → peak-profile fitting → residual assessment → structural descriptor extraction. XPS schematic showing a spectral envelope, fitted components, and background. Open XPS schematic XPS · Schematic Enlarge image Surface-chemical descriptors XPS Survey quantification describes surface composition. High-resolution envelope fitting examines relative contributions from selected chemical environments. Elemental ratios Quantified atomic-fraction ratios, including F/Ti where available. Describe relative surface composition. Binding energy Position of a fitted spectral contribution. Supports chemical-environment interpretation with calibration and assignment controls. Component fraction A component’s share of the fitted envelope area. Compares modelled chemical contributions within that region. TiOₓ-like fraction A model-dependent contribution associated with selected oxidized titanium environments. Fitting: background alternatives, constrained components, linked spin–orbit partners, and residual checks. Survey composition remains distinct from envelope fractions. Raman schematic illustrating peak shift, linewidth, and integrated spectral contribution. Open Raman schematic Raman · Schematic Enlarge image Vibrational descriptors Raman Spectroscopy Corresponding vibrational features are fitted to quantify frequency displacement, broadening, and relative spectral contributions. Peak shift, Δω Frequency change relative to a defined reference. Tracks changes in the selected vibrational environment. Linewidth, Γ Width of a fitted vibrational feature. Describes broadening that can reflect disorder and other mode-dependent effects. Integrated area Signal beneath a fitted feature. Supports controlled comparisons of spectral contributions. Normalized shift Rescaled selected Raman shift. Supplies the vibrational variable used in the composite descriptor framework. MATLAB: spectral processing → corresponding-feature identification → peak fitting. Absolute intensity depends on acquisition conditions. FTIR transmittance schematic showing downward absorption bands and selected integration regions. Open FTIR schematic FTIR transmittance · Schematic Enlarge image Integrated spectral descriptors FTIR Transmittance bands visualize infrared absorption. For descriptor extraction, corrected absorbance provides defined band areas and comparative spectral ratios. Band position Wavenumber of a selected absorption feature. Helps identify and compare vibrational regions. Band areas, B1–B4 Integrated corrected absorbance over defined windows. Quantifies each selected spectral contribution. B2 area fraction Relative contribution of the termination-sensitive region. Provides an interface-sensitive descriptor. Band-area ratios B2/B1, B3/B1, and B4/B1 compare termination-, adsorbate-, and hydroxyl-sensitive regions with the lattice-related window. Processing: when starting from transmittance, A = −log₁₀(T), with T expressed as a fraction. Baseline-corrected absorbance is integrated. The displayed schematic remains in transmittance. Gas-sorption schematic showing adsorption, desorption, hysteresis, and a porous solid. Open BET schematic BET / gas sorption · Schematic Enlarge image Accessible interface descriptors BET & Gas Sorption Gas-sorption analysis describes accessible surface area and pore geometry. Derived variables provide inputs for interface and effective-transport models. Surface area, SBET Gas-accessible area per unit mass. Describes the interface available to the adsorptive probe. entries.title: Electrochemical Modelling
entries.description: Explore CV, EIS, and GCD analysis, equivalent-circuit models, state-space simulation, and MATLAB workflows for electrochemical response modelling.
entries.headings: Electrochemical Modelling Cyclic Voltammetry Integrate the complete response Separate common background current Power-law and two-term analysis Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy Describe resistance and relaxation Re-express the measured impedance Galvanostatic Charge–Discharge Quantify resolved charge–discharge segments From circuit topology to simulated response Use capacitor voltages as states Separate empirical rate laws from circuit models. The modelling sequence.
entries.text: Skip to content Research / Modelling / Electrochemical Electrochemical Modelling I model electrochemical charge storage through complementary analyses of cyclic voltammetry, impedance spectroscopy, and galvanostatic charge–discharge. The framework separates directly extracted descriptors, empirical rate relationships, and physical circuit models. MATLAB simulations connect resistance, storage, leakage, and relaxation times with complete measured curves. CV models EIS models GCD models Circuit simulation Model assessment MATLAB workflow Page sections Schematic showing cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and galvanostatic charge–discharge CV · EIS · GCD — Schematic View full image Potential-controlled response Cyclic Voltammetry Descriptor / Loop capacitance Integrate the complete response Anodic and cathodic branches are interpolated onto a common potential grid before integration. The potential window and scan rate remain explicit. This summarizes stored-charge response across the selected potential interval. C(ν) = [1/(2νΔV)] ∫VlowVhigh [ia(V) − ic(V)] dV ΔV = Vhigh − Vlow ν is the scan rate. ia and ic are corresponding branch currents. Specific or areal capacitance requires the corresponding mass or area normalization. Processing / Branch separation Separate common background current The branch average describes common-direction background, while the half-difference isolates the symmetric response used for rate analysis. A shared background can bias power-law fits performed on one branch alone. ibg(V) = [ia(V) + ic(V)]/2 is(V) = [ia(V) − ic(V)]/2 Cancellation applies to a contribution shared by both branches; it is not a universal separation of all electrochemical processes. Models / Scan-rate dependence Power-law and two-term analysis The power law describes current scaling. The Dunn-type decomposition represents terms proportional to scan rate and its square root. These provide operational rate descriptors for comparable potentials and measurement sessions. is(V,ν) = a(V)νb(V) is(V,ν) = k1(V)ν + k2(V)ν1/2 b describes rate scaling. k1 and k2 are operational decomposition coefficients. Conventional surface-like or diffusion-like interpretations do not prove a mechanism. Trasatti charge-accessibility analysis Slow- and fast-rate extrapolations provide operational outer and total charge estimates within appropriate fitting ranges. q(ν) = qout + c1ν−1/2 1/q(ν) = 1/qtot + c2ν1/2 The ratio qout/qtot is an accessibility descriptor. The validity of the extrapolation depends on the selected rate domain. Frequency-dependent response Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy Model / Equivalent circuits Describe resistance and relaxation Candidate networks combine series resistance, storage branches, and non-ideal capacitive elements. Circuit labels identify mathematical branches rather than predetermined mechanisms. These connect frequency dependence with interpretable resistance and timescale parameters. ZCPE(ω) = 1/[Q(jω)n] τRC = RC τR‖CPE = (RQ)1/n Q and n define the constant-phase element. Q is not directly a capacitance when n differs from one. Descriptor / Complex capacitance Re-express the measured impedance Complex capacitance supplies a complementary representation of storage and loss across frequency. Its interpretation remains tied to the impedance definition and any resistance correction. C*(ω) = 1/[jωZ(ω)] C*(ω) = C′(ω) − jC″(ω) Additional descriptors include the high-frequency real-axis intercept, low-frequency impedance, phase, and characteristic relaxation measures. Linear Kramers–Kronig checks and residual inspection support assessment of spectral consistency. A visually plausible circuit fit alone does not establish parameter identifiability. Current-controlled response Galvanostatic Charge–Discharge Descriptors / Time, charge, and energy Quantify resolved charge–discharge segments Segment duration, potential window, and applied current define apparent capacitance. Charge and energy integration provide complementary efficiency measures. These distinguish charge recovery from voltage-dependent energy recovery. Cchg = |Ichg|Δtchg/ΔV Cdis = |Idis|Δtdis/ΔV ηQ = |qdis|/|qchg| E = ∫VI dt Potential windows, resistive jumps, current signs, and normalization conventions are defined explicitly. Physical curve reconstruction From circuit topology to simulated response Within each multi-rate CV or GCD fit, one parameter set describes the complete family of curves. Rate dependence therefore emerges from circuit time constants rather than independent parameters assigned to every scan rate or current. Element Representation Purpose Rs Series resistance Ohmic contribution; constrained using EIS from the corresponding electrode. Ri ‖ Ci Relaxation branch Access-limited response with τi = RiCi. C3 Fully accessed storage capacitance Low-rate storage contribution. Rp Leakage path across the storage network Tests whether a conductive parasitic path is needed by the observations. CPE Distributed capacitive response Describes non-ideal relaxation over a range of timescales. Equivalent-circuit elements; scroll horizontally on small screens Numerical model / State space Use capacitor voltages as states Finite RC networks are expressed as linear dynamical systems. The excitation changes between CV and GCD while the circuit equations retain their physical structure. This supports direct simulation of complete waveforms rather than only summary descriptors. dx/dt = Ax + bI V = cᵀx + DI x contains internal capacitor voltages. Matrices and vectors follow from the candidate topology. CV simulation: piecewise linear potential ramps For nonzero feedthrough D, potential control eliminates current from the state equations. Each linear sweep is propagated using the analytical linear-system solution. V(t) = V0 + st, s = ±ν I = (V − cᵀx)/D Initial state, cycle count, and sampling follow the experimental protocol. Analytical propagation avoids an arbitrary time-step approximation for the finite linear network. GCD simulation: constant-current segments Constant applied current drives the state equations. Charge and discharge segments are propagated to the defined potential boundaries, with switching and initial conditions retained explicitly. CPE realization: distributed timescales A CPE has no exact finite-dimensional state-space realization. I use a discretized relaxation-time distribution to construct a finite approximation over the experimental window. The numerical realization is checked against the analytical impedance before being used for time-domain simulation. Model choice and interpretation Separate empirical rate laws from circuit models. Empirical functions summarize capacitance versus scan rate or current. Circuit models instead aim to explain the complete curve family through shared physical parameters. Representative candidate rate laws C(x) = C0 C(x) = Ax−β C(x) = C∞ + Ax−β x denotes the relevant measurement rate. Here β is a fitted rate exponent, unrelated to TGA heating-rate notation. Model assessment considers parameter identifiability, bounds, residual structure, information criteria, bootstrap uncertainty, and withheld scan rates, currents, or frequencies. Extra circuit branches require support beyond improved visual agreement. Cross-technique comparison examines compatible resistance and relaxation scales. It does not assume that every technique must return identical apparent capacitance or share one independently untested fit. MATLAB implementation The modelling sequence. Import and check the measurements Preserve electrode identity, acquisition session, cycle selection, potential windows, scan rates, currents, and frequencies. Extract model-independent descriptors Calculate CV loop measures, branch-separated currents, impedance descriptors, and resolved charge–discharge quantities. Fit rate relationships Compare candidate functions using consistent observation windows and normalization. Construct candidate storage networks Compare blocking, relaxing, distributed, and leakage-containing topologies. Simulate the experimental excitation Apply piecewise potential ramps or current steps with the stated initial conditions and switching rules. Fit shared parameters within each curve family Let rate dependence emerge from the model rather than fitting independent parameters at every rate. Assess identifiability and predictive checks Examine residuals, parameter stability, bootstrap intervals, and appropriate withheld observations. Verify the numerical implementation Compare limiting cases with analytical RC and leaky-capacitor expressions, and check CPE approximations against analytical impedance. ← Back to modelling Electrochemical experiments → Rupesh Lal Karn Prairie View, Texas rkarn@pvamu.edu Google Scholar ORCID CV Projects Contact Academic profiles © 2026 Rupesh Lal Karn

entries.headings: From circuit topology to simulated response Use capacitor voltages as states
entries.text: Physical curve reconstruction From circuit topology to simulated response Within each multi-rate CV or GCD fit, one parameter set describes the complete family of curves. Rate dependence therefore emerges from circuit time constants rather than independent parameters assigned to every scan rate or current. Element Representation Purpose Rs Series resistance Ohmic contribution; constrained using EIS from the corresponding electrode. Ri ‖ Ci Relaxation branch Access-limited response with τi = RiCi. C3 Fully accessed storage capacitance Low-rate storage contribution. Rp Leakage path across the storage network Tests whether a conductive parasitic path is needed by the observations. CPE Distributed capacitive response Describes non-ideal relaxation over a range of timescales. Equivalent-circuit elements; scroll horizontally on small screens Numerical model / State space Use capacitor voltages as states Finite RC networks are expressed as linear dynamical systems. The excitation changes between CV and GCD while the circuit equations retain their physical structure. This supports direct simulation of complete waveforms rather than only summary descriptors. dx/dt = Ax + bI V = cᵀx + DI x contains internal capacitor voltages. Matrices and vectors follow from the candidate topology. CV simulation: piecewise linear potential ramps For nonzero feedthrough D, potential control eliminates current from the state equations. Each linear sweep is propagated using the analytical linear-system solution. V(t) = V0 + st, s = ±ν I = (V − cᵀx)/D Initial state, cycle count, and sampling follow the experimental protocol. Analytical propagation avoids an arbitrary time-step approximation for the finite linear network. GCD simulation: constant-current segments Constant applied current drives the state equations. Charge and discharge segments are propagated to the defined potential boundaries, with switching and initial conditions retained explicitly. CPE realization: distributed timescales A CPE has no exact finite-dimensional state-space realization. I use a discretized relaxation-time distribution to construct a finite approximation over the experimental window. The numerical realization is checked against the analytical impedance before being used for time-domain simulation.

entries.headings: Separate empirical rate laws from circuit models.
entries.text: Model choice and interpretation Separate empirical rate laws from circuit models. Empirical functions summarize capacitance versus scan rate or current. Circuit models instead aim to explain the complete curve family through shared physical parameters. Representative candidate rate laws C(x) = C0 C(x) = Ax−β C(x) = C∞ + Ax−β x denotes the relevant measurement rate. Here β is a fitted rate exponent, unrelated to TGA heating-rate notation. Model assessment considers parameter identifiability, bounds, residual structure, information criteria, bootstrap uncertainty, and withheld scan rates, currents, or frequencies. Extra circuit branches require support beyond improved visual agreement. Cross-technique comparison examines compatible resistance and relaxation scales. It does not assume that every technique must return identical apparent capacitance or share one independently untested fit.

entries.text: Skip to content Research / Photothermal & Electrochemical Studies Electrochemical Studies I investigate electrode response through complementary measurements of current, potential, time, and frequency. Cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and galvanostatic charge–discharge provide connected views of charge storage, resistance, and relaxation. Research focus Techniques Comparison strategy Experimental workflow Page sections Research question How does the electrode respond across timescales? Electrochemical behaviour depends on the measurement timescale as well as the material. Complementary techniques help distinguish apparent charge storage, resistive contributions, and delayed access to the response. My approach compares complete measurement profiles alongside extracted quantities, including changes associated with cycling. Storage How much charge is accessed within the selected potential window and measurement duration? Relaxation Which response times influence frequency dependence and rate accessibility? Evolution How do measured profiles and derived quantities change across the defined cycling protocol? Complementary measurements Three techniques, different experimental questions. CV Cyclic voltammetry Measurement Current during controlled forward and reverse potential sweeps. Quantities examined Loop shape, branch currents, integrated charge, apparent capacitance, and scan-rate dependence. EIS Impedance spectroscopy Measurement Small-signal response across frequency. Quantities examined Real and imaginary impedance, phase, resistance scales, and distributed relaxation. GCD Galvanostatic charge–discharge Measurement Potential evolution under defined current segments. Quantities examined Charge–discharge duration, apparent capacitance, charge balance, energy, and voltage changes. These techniques provide operational descriptors under defined conditions. A curve shape, scan-rate exponent, or equivalent-circuit fit alone does not establish a unique mechanism. Comparison strategy Keep the experimental definitions consistent. Document the electrode and measurement state Retain material identity, preparation details, normalization basis, and cycling history. Acquire complementary responses Measure CV, EIS, and GCD using defined potential, current, and frequency protocols. Check measurement quality Inspect clipping, drift, resolved segments, repeatability where available, and spectral consistency. Extract comparable quantities Calculate charge, capacitance, impedance, and rate-related measures with explicit conventions. Interpret across techniques Compare storage and relaxation information while retaining the different timescales and assumptions. Explore the models behind the response. Laxman Palikhel Institution Thapathali Campus, Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University Funded experimental research · Jatropha biodiesel Testing of Performance Characteristics and Emission Improvement of Jatropha Oil in Internal Combustion Engines Abstract An experimental investigation was carried out to study the performance of Jatropha blends the test bench. The fuel thermo-physical properties of Jatropha blend 20% (JB20) was tested. The test result showed that the properties of JB20 are under the Biodiesel Standard India. Cetane number of JB20 was found higher than that of standard Cetane number of diesel and Cetane number of Bharat Biodiesel standard which leads to improving ignition quality by pre-ignition timing. Higher water content in Jatropha blends facilitate in combustion process. The performance of various Jatropha blend with pure diesel up to 20% were tested. There is a small margin of difference between the Brake power of various Jatropha blends and Diesel. JB20 has better performance parameters such indicated power, brake power, indicated thermal efficiency, brake thermal efficiency, specific fuel consumption, and fuel consumption than other Jatropha blends. So JB20 can be used as an alternative fuel in internal combustion engines. All the blends of Jatropha oil passed the opacity test. Related undergraduate fuel research → University Grant Commission UGC · Nepal Programme Small RDI Grant Grant reference SRDI-75/76-Engg-3 Grant year 2075/76 B.S. Progress report 1 February 2020 My role Research Assistant Principal investigator Er. Laxman Palikhel Funded experimental research · Waste-plastic-derived fuel Testing of Performance Characteristics and Emission Improvement of Plastic Pyrolysis Fuel in Internal Combustion Engines Abstract An experimental investigation was carried out to study the performance of Plasto diesel blends in test bench. The fuel thermo-physical properties of Plasto diesel blend 10% (PDB10) and Plasto diesel blend 20% (PDB20) were tested. Test result showed that the properties of Plasto diesel are under the Bharat Standard 4 and Bharat standard 6. Cetane number of PDB10 and PDB20 was found higher than that of standard which leads to improve ignition quality by pre-ignition timing. The performance and Combustion Characteristics of various Plasto diesel blend with pure diesel up to 20% were tested. For the same brake power, the indicated power of 20PDB is lower than conventional diesel. There is a small margin of difference in IP of other blends of PDB and Diesel. There is a small margin of difference in Specific fuel consumption of 20PDB and Diesel. Mechanical efficiency of 20PDB is greater than other blends of Plasto diesel and conventional diesel, volumetric efficiency of 20PDB is lower than other blends of Plasto Diesel and Diesel. 20PDB has lower ignition delay and the cylinder pressure of Plasto diesel blends is lower than diesel, all the blends of Plastodiesel blend passed the opacity test. From the fuel property and engine performance, combustion and emission characteristics, it is concluded that any blends of plastic oil up to 20PDB can be used as an alternative source of conventional diesel. Plastic-derived fuel research → Thapathali Campus Institute of Engineering · Tribhuvan University Support Institutional research grant Report date March 2025 My role Co-Principal Investigator (Co-PI) Project supervisor Er. Laxman Palikhel Institutionally supported research · Hybrid biodiesel & modelling Optimizing Sustainable Hybrid Biodiesel: A Synergistic Blend of Soybean and Sesame Oils for Enhanced Engine Performance, Combustion and Emission Abstract This study aims to test and optimize the performance of hybrid biodiesel composed of soybean and sesame as a potential alternative for diesel fuel. This research involves characterization of sesame and soybean biodiesel, testing and analysis of performance parameters, combustion and emission characteristics of sesame biodiesel and soybean biodiesel blends. The research also focuses on using Matlab to construct a model and simulate it for various blends of various biodiesel. Simulation of the model constructed is then validated by comparing with result obtained from experiment performed on test engine. The test engine used was a single cylinder four stroke water-cooled diesel engine fitted with eddy current dynamometer operating at constant speed of 1500 RPM. For the characterization of sesame and soybean biodiesel, FTIR and GCMS was done. Major fatty acid methyl ester component of sesame and soybean biodiesel was found to be methyl oleate and methyl linoleate. For sesame biodiesel, 10SBME was found to be the optimized blend. This is because it had better performance, combustion and emission than other blends in overall. For soybean biodiesel, 20SME and 30SME were found to be the optimized blend because it had better performance, combustion and emission than other blends in overall. On the basis of performance characteristics, 30SME is better while on the basis of emission, 20SME had better result. For hybrid biodiesel, it was found that 20-20SeSoD had maximum decrease in specific fuel consumption by 2.62%, EGT by 9.92% and highest brake thermal efficiency by 3.72%. so, it can be considered as optimal blend but cost of 20-20 SeSoD is higher than that of diesel making it economically expensive fuel. So, we do not consider it optimal blend. The optimal blend for hybrid biodiesel is considered 10-20SeSoD as it is cheaper and also has better overall better performance. Combustion and emission than diesel. Also, it had maximum decrease in Indicated power by 2.46%, slight increase in SFC by 0.75%, increase in brake thermal efficiency and mechanical efficiency by 4.13% in average compared to diesel. 10-20SeSoD also has least CPM with decrease of 5.69%, but has decrease in CHR by 10.50% while it has least NO and NOx emission. NO, Nox and HC emission for 10-20SeSoD decreased by 20.37%, 19.29% and 65.41% in average compared to diesel. So, in terms of emission, it has drastic benefit. AEPC · Jatropha biodiesel UGC · Plastic pyrolysis fuel Thapathali Campus · Hybrid biodiesel Funded research projects Alternative Energy Promotion Centre AEPC · Government of Nepal Report date 22 June 2019 My role Research Assistant Project supervisor Er. Laxman Palikhel Institution Thapathali Campus, Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University Funded experimental research · Jatropha biodiesel Testing of Performance Characteristics and Emission Improvement of Jatropha Oil in Internal Combustion Engines Abstract An experimental investigation was carried out to study the performance of Jatropha blends the test bench. The fuel thermo-physical properties of Jatropha blend 20% (JB20) was tested. The test result showed that the properties of JB20 are under the Biodiesel Standard India. Cetane number of JB20 was found higher than that of standard Cetane number of diesel and Cetane number of Bharat Biodiesel standard which leads to improving ignition quality by pre-ignition timing. Higher water content in Jatropha blends facilitate in combustion process. The performance of various Jatropha blend with pure diesel up to 20% were tested. There is a small margin of difference between the Brake power of various Jatropha blends and Diesel. JB20 has better performance parameters such indicated power, brake power, indicated thermal efficiency, brake thermal efficiency, specific fuel consumption, and fuel consumption than other Jatropha blends. So JB20 can be used as an alternative fuel in internal combustion engines. All the blends of Jatropha oil passed the opacity test. Related undergraduate fuel research → University Grant Commission UGC · Nepal Programme Small RDI Grant Grant reference SRDI-75/76-Engg-3 Grant year 2075/76 B.S. Progress report 1 February 2020 My role Research Assistant Principal investigator Er. Laxman Palikhel Funded experimental research · Waste-plastic-derived fuel Testing of Performance Characteristics and Emission Improvement of Plastic Pyrolysis Fuel in Internal Combustion Engines Abstract An experimental investigation was carried out to study the performance of Plasto diesel blends in test bench. The fuel thermo-physical properties of Plasto diesel blend 10% (PDB10) and Plasto diesel blend 20% (PDB20) were tested. Test result showed that the properties of Plasto diesel are under the Bharat Standard 4 and Bharat standard 6. Cetane number of PDB10 and PDB20 was found higher than that of standard which leads to improve ignition quality by pre-ignition timing. The performance and Combustion Characteristics of various Plasto diesel blend with pure diesel up to 20% were tested. For the same brake power, the indicated power of 20PDB is lower than conventional diesel. There is a small margin of difference in IP of other blends of PDB and Diesel. There is a small margin of difference in Specific fuel consumption of 20PDB and Diesel. Mechanical efficiency of 20PDB is greater than other blends of Plasto diesel and conventional diesel, volumetric efficiency of 20PDB is lower than other blends of Plasto Diesel and Diesel. 20PDB has lower ignition delay and the cylinder pressure of Plasto diesel blends is lower than diesel, all the blends of Plastodiesel blend passed the opacity test. From the fuel property and engine performance, combustion and emission characteristics, it is concluded that any blends of plastic oil up to 20PDB can be used as an alternative source of conventional diesel. Plastic-derived fuel research → Thapathali Campus Institute of Engineering · Tribhuvan University Support Institutional research grant Report date March 2025 My role Co-Principal Investigator (Co-PI) Project supervisor Er. Laxman Palikhel Institutionally supported research · Hybrid biodiesel & modelling Optimizing Sustainable Hybrid Biodiesel: A Synergistic Blend of Soybean and Sesame Oils for Enhanced Engine Performance, Combustion and Emission Abstract This study aims to test and optimize the performance of hybrid biodiesel composed of soybean and sesame as a potential alternative for diesel fuel. This research involves characterization of sesame and soybean biodiesel, testing and analysis of performance parameters, combustion and emission characteristics of sesame biodiesel and soybean biodiesel blends. The research also focuses on using Matlab to construct a model and simulate it for various blends of various biodiesel. Simulation of the model constructed is then validated by comparing with result obtained from experiment performed on test engine. The test engine used was a single cylinder four stroke water-cooled diesel engine fitted with eddy current dynamometer operating at constant speed of 1500 RPM. For the characterization of sesame and soybean biodiesel, FTIR and GCMS was done. Major fatty acid methyl ester component of sesame and soybean biodiesel was found to be methyl oleate and methyl linoleate. For sesame biodiesel, 10SBME was found to be the optimized blend. This is because it had better performance, combustion and emission than other blends in overall. For soybean biodiesel, 20SME and 30SME were found to be the optimized blend because it had better performance, combustion and emission than other blends in overall. On the basis of performance characteristics, 30SME is better while on the basis of emission, 20SME had better result. For hybrid biodiesel, it was found that 20-20SeSoD had maximum decrease in specific fuel consumption by 2.62%, EGT by 9.92% and highest brake thermal efficiency by 3.72%. so, it can be considered as optimal blend but cost of 20-20 SeSoD is higher than that of diesel making it economically expensive fuel. So, we do not consider it optimal blend. The optimal blend for hybrid biodiesel is considered 10-20SeSoD as it is cheaper and also has better overall better performance. Combustion and emission than diesel. Also, it had maximum decrease in Indicated power by 2.46%, slight increase in SFC by 0.75%, increase in brake thermal efficiency and mechanical efficiency by 4.13% in average compared to diesel. 10-20SeSoD also has least CPM with decrease of 5.69%, but has decrease in CHR by 10.50% while it has least NO and NOx emission. NO, Nox and HC emission for 10-20SeSoD decreased by 20.37%, 19.29% and 65.41% in average compared to diesel. So, in terms of emission, it has drastic benefit. Student research team: Gagin Bajagain, Lasata Maharjan, Samjhana Jyakhwo, and Sushila Subedi. Biodiesel research →

entries.text: Skip to content Engineering projects / GOKART Undergraduate automotive engineering project GOKART Engine modification, mechanical integration, and assembly of an existing go-kart. This project connects workshop engineering with a practical vehicle demonstration. Engine replacement · Spark-ignition engine · Mechanical integration · Vehicle assembly A driver operating the go-kart on a paved outdoor court with observers nearby View original go-kart driving demonstration photograph Driving demonstration The assembled go-kart in operation The assembled go-kart during an outdoor driving demonstration, documenting the practical application of the engine modification and mechanical integration work. View original photograph → Project background Reworking an existing vehicle. This automotive engineering project involved modifying an existing go-kart by replacing its generator engine with a spark-ignition engine. The work focused on integrating the replacement engine with the existing vehicle and assembling its mechanical components. The photographs document the go-kart in the workshop, its exposed component layout outdoors, and a driving demonstration. They show the relationship between the chassis, driver’s seat, steering arrangement, and rear-mounted engine. Engine replacement Replacement of the existing generator engine with a spark-ignition engine as the central modification to the go-kart. entries.text: Project background Reworking an existing vehicle. This automotive engineering project involved modifying an existing go-kart by replacing its generator engine with a spark-ignition engine. The work focused on integrating the replacement engine with the existing vehicle and assembling its mechanical components. The photographs document the go-kart in the workshop, its exposed component layout outdoors, and a driving demonstration. They show the relationship between the chassis, driver’s seat, steering arrangement, and rear-mounted engine. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Magnetic Materials & Crystal Growth 04 / Magnetic Materials · Graduate Research Magnetic Materials & Crystal Growth My research includes magnetic-powder synthesis, compositional doping, single-crystal growth, structural refinement, and magnetic characterization. Material systems include cobalt-substituted MnGeTeO₆ and Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ single crystals, alongside national-laboratory experience in magnetic-domain imaging and quantum-oscillation measurements. Synthesis Magnetic Powders & Compositional Doping Crystal Growth Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ Single Crystals Advanced Characterization SQUID · LTEM · dHvA Material Systems Synthesis & Growth Characterization National Laboratories Page sections 01 / MATERIAL SYSTEMS Material Systems My work combines preparation and characterization to investigate how material composition and structure relate to magnetic behaviour. Powder synthesis, doping, and single-crystal growth provide complementary routes to these questions. Cobalt-Substituted Magnetic Oxide Mn1−xCoxGeTeO6 MnGeTeO₆ host Co Substitution Composition-Dependent Study Co-Doped MnGeTeO₆ I worked on cobalt substitution in MnGeTeO₆, expressed through the composition Mn₁₋ₓCoₓGeTeO₆. The substitution level x defines the nominal replacement of Mn by Co. The research combines material preparation with structural and magnetic characterization. Comparing compositions provides a route to investigate changes in phase formation, crystallographic parameters, and magnetic response. Single-Crystal Material Mn3Al2Ge3O12 Single-Crystal Growth Magnetic Oxide Structural Characterization Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ Single Crystals My experience includes growing Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ single crystals and preparing samples for subsequent characterization. Single-crystal specimens complement powder studies by providing well-defined samples for structural and physical-property investigations. Sample identity, preparation history, and measurement geometry remain important when connecting crystal preparation with measured behaviour. 02 / EXPERIMENTAL PREPARATION Synthesis, Doping & Crystal Growth Magnetic-Powder Synthesis Experience with magnetic-powder preparation and solid-state synthesis, connecting precursor composition and processing history with subsequent phase characterization. Compositional Doping Preparation of cobalt-substituted MnGeTeO₆ compositions, with nominal substitution recorded explicitly for comparison across samples. Single-Crystal Growth Growth of Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ single crystals, alongside sample preparation and characterization for materials research. 03 / STRUCTURE–PROPERTY INVESTIGATION Structural & Magnetic Characterization My research at Prairie View A&M University, including NSF-supported work supervised by Dr. Sunil Karna, involved synthesis and structural refinement of magnetic materials and crystals. Technique Information Examined Research Role X-ray diffraction Crystalline phases and diffraction profiles Evaluate phase formation and structural differences between prepared samples Rietveld refinement Crystallographic parameters supported by the diffraction data Compare structural models and composition-dependent structural changes Raman spectroscopy Vibrational features associated with bonding and symmetry Complement diffraction-based interpretation SQUID magnetometry Magnetic response under defined temperature and field conditions Investigate magnetic behaviour with explicit measurement protocols Lorentz TEM Magnetic-domain-related electron contrast Examine spatial magnetic structures dHvA measurements Angle- and temperature-dependent quantum oscillations Investigate electronic structure in single-crystal HfSn₂ 04 / VISITING RESEARCH EXPERIENCE National Laboratory Measurements 23 JUNE – 4 JULY 2025 Argonne National Laboratory Visiting Research Student Magnetic-Domain Investigation Using LTEM Performed advanced Lorentz transmission electron microscopy analysis to investigate magnetic domain structures. LTEM provides spatial information that complements bulk magnetic measurements. Interpretation considers imaging conditions, specimen geometry, and non-magnetic contrast contributions. 4–15 AUGUST 2025 Los Alamos National Laboratory Visiting Research Student Quantum Oscillations in HfSn₂ Performed angle- and temperature-dependent de Haas–van Alphen measurements on HfSn₂ crystals. Angular dependence provides information relevant to Fermi-surface geometry, while temperature-dependent amplitudes support effective-mass analysis under the appropriate measurement and modelling conditions. This work concerns quantum-oscillation measurements on HfSn₂, distinct from my oxide synthesis and Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ crystal-growth activities. Preparation, Structure & Physical Response My experience connects magnetic-powder synthesis, cobalt substitution, and single-crystal growth with structural refinement and advanced magnetic and electronic measurements. LTEM provides spatial information that complements bulk magnetic measurements. Interpretation considers imaging conditions, specimen geometry, and non-magnetic contrast contributions. 4–15 AUGUST 2025 Los Alamos National Laboratory Visiting Research Student Quantum Oscillations in HfSn₂ Performed angle- and temperature-dependent de Haas–van Alphen measurements on HfSn₂ crystals. Angular dependence provides information relevant to Fermi-surface geometry, while temperature-dependent amplitudes support effective-mass analysis under the appropriate measurement and modelling conditions. This work concerns quantum-oscillation measurements on HfSn₂, distinct from my oxide synthesis and Mn₃Al₂Ge₃O₁₂ crystal-growth activities.

entries.headings: Photothermal Modelling Three terms describe the transient. Heat input Thermal storage Heat loss Heating and cooling tell different parts of the story. Heating response Cooling response Give the heat estimate a defined scale. Each parameter has a specific meaning. From temperature records to thermal parameters. Connecting response to material properties
entries.text: Skip to content Research / Modelling / Photothermal Photothermal Modelling Photothermal modelling translates measured heating and cooling curves into response times, thermal amplitudes, and reference-calibrated heat-input estimates. The analysis fits laser-on and laser-off segments separately and retains a clear distinction between measured, fitted, extrapolated, and reference-calibrated quantities. Energy balance Heating & cooling Calibration Extracted quantities MATLAB workflow Page sections The physical model Three terms describe the transient. A representative bulk temperature describes the suspension. Effective thermal capacity accounts for storage, while a combined heat-loss conductance describes exchange with the surroundings. Photothermal schematic showing heating, laser switch-off, cooling, and heat-transfer pathways. Photothermal transient model · Schematic View full image → Heat input The effective rate of thermal energy supplied during irradiation. Thermal storage Energy accumulation associated with the changing system temperature. Heat loss Effective environmental loss proportional to the temperature rise. Csys dΔT/dt = Qin − HΔT ΔT = T − Tamb, H = hA Csys: thermal capacity, J K⁻¹ · Qin: heat-input rate, W · H: effective heat-loss conductance, W K⁻¹. Assumptions: representative bulk temperature, approximately constant thermal properties and laser input, effective linear heat loss, negligible evaporation, and cessation of irradiation-induced input at switch-off. Fit the two segments Heating and cooling tell different parts of the story. Laser on Heating response The fitted curve describes the approach toward an asymptotic rise under constant effective conditions. ΔT(t) = ΔT∞ [1 − exp(−t/τH)] τH: heating timescale. ΔT∞: model-extrapolated asymptotic rise. This form assumes zero initial temperature rise. For a nonzero initial rise, retain its exponential term. Laser off Cooling response Once irradiation ends, the temperature decays toward ambient through effective environmental loss. ΔT(t) = ΔToff exp[−(t − toff)/τC] τC: cooling timescale. ΔToff: rise at switch-off. The ideal lumped relation is τ = Csys/H. Heating and cooling times are fitted separately. The temperature reached at switch-off and the fitted asymptotic temperature are distinct quantities. An asymptote does not imply that equilibrium was reached during the experiment. Water-reference calibration Give the heat estimate a defined scale. Water cooling supplies a reference heat-loss conductance. Comparative sample calculations use that scale with explicit thermal-capacity assumptions. Csys = mliqcp + Ccontainer Hwater = Csys,water/τC,water Qnet,off = Hwater [ΔTsample,off − ΔTwater,off] The container contribution is not independently available and is set to zero in this calculation. The resulting calibration therefore uses nominal liquid thermal capacity. The switch-off estimator assumes compatible geometry and effective heat-loss behaviour. It remains distinct from equilibrium input or intrinsic conversion efficiency. Extracted quantities Each parameter has a specific meaning. Measured, fitted, and derived quantities remain identifiable. Units, fitting intervals, material mass, and reference conditions accompany the values. Quantity What it describes Type ΔToff Temperature rise at the irradiation endpoint Finite-time response ΔT∞ Asymptotic temperature rise from the heating fit Model extrapolation τH, τC Heating and cooling response times Fitted parameters 1/τH, 1/τC Reciprocal response times Derived rate measures ∫ΔT(t) dt Temperature-rise area over a stated interval Integrated transient measure Qnet,off Water-calibrated switch-off estimator Comparative heat-input quantity Qnet,off / mp Heat-input estimator per dispersed material mass Mass-normalized quantity Photothermal model quantities; scroll horizontally on small screens MATLAB workflow From temperature records to thermal parameters. Prepare the records Align time, temperature, laser switching, concentration, material mass, and water-reference data. Define the baseline Establish ambient temperature and calculate the temperature rise. Select fitting intervals Separate heating and cooling using the irradiation boundaries. Fit the transients Estimate amplitudes and separate time constants. Positive parameters can use logarithmic coordinates. Apply the calibration Combine the water cooling timescale with the stated nominal thermal capacity. Extract response measures Calculate switch-off rise, transient area, time constants, and comparative heat-input quantities. Inspect uncertainty Examine residual autocorrelation, systematic deviations, parameter stability, and fitting-window sensitivity. Check physical consistency Verify units, initial conditions, ambient recovery, and the distinction between measured and extrapolated quantities. Connecting response to material properties The extracted thermal quantities provide response targets for the separate physics-guided descriptor framework. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Photothermal & Electrochemical Studies Photothermal Studies I investigate how material processing and suspension concentration influence heating and cooling under near-infrared irradiation. The experimental framework connects controlled temperature measurements with characterization of structure, surface chemistry, and dispersion. Research focus Material series Experimental approach Measurements Page sections Research question How does processing change the thermal response? Chemical etching and intercalation alter material structure and interfaces. Photothermal measurements examine the associated temperature response under defined irradiation conditions. The study considers both the rise during irradiation and the subsequent cooling, rather than relying only on an endpoint temperature. Schematic photothermal heating and cooling with irradiation and heat-loss pathways. Heating–cooling response · Schematic Enlarge image Material series Follow the processing sequence. MAX precursor Ti₃AlCN provides the precursor reference for comparing processing-dependent changes. Acid-etched MXene Ti₃CNTₓ represents the etched material state, with structure and surface chemistry examined through complementary characterization. DMSO-treated MXene The treated state extends the comparison to processing-related changes in stacking, interfaces, and dispersion. Experimental approach Measure the complete irradiation cycle. Prepare the suspensions Retain material identity, concentration, suspension volume, and preparation history. Establish the baseline Record the initial temperature and maintain consistent vessel and irradiation geometry. Apply near-infrared irradiation Track the temperature continuously during the defined laser-on interval. Record cooling Continue measuring after switch-off to characterize the return toward ambient. Measure the water reference Use comparable conditions to distinguish the suspension response from the reference background. Quantities of interest Read the transient at several levels. Observation What it describes Interpretation Temperature rise Change relative to the ambient baseline Finite-time heating response Heating profile Evolution during irradiation Rate and shape of the temperature increase Cooling profile Evolution after switch-off Effective loss-controlled response Concentration comparison Response across suspension loadings Condition-dependent behaviour Processing comparison Response across the material series Context for comparison with characterization and dispersion measurements Photothermal measurements table; scroll horizontally on small screens A larger measured temperature rise alone does not establish a larger intrinsic conversion efficiency. Geometry, thermal capacity, heat loss, concentration, and absorbed optical power affect interpretation. Explore the analysis behind the measurements. The dedicated modelling page explains the energy balance, heating–cooling fits, water calibration, thermal descriptors, and uncertainty assessment. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Modelling / Physics-guided descriptors Physics-Guided Descriptor Modelling I connect material characterization with measured response through interpretable descriptors, explicit assumptions, and compact mathematical relationships. Characterization-derived variables are screened and normalized before they enter a response model. Physical reasoning guides their definitions, the candidate relationships, and the limits of interpretation. Framework Screening Descriptor families Response modelling Assessment MATLAB workflow Page sections The modelling framework From characterization to a physical question. My framework organizes characterization-derived variables before fitting response relationships. Physical reasoning guides the inputs, transformations, targets, and interpretation. Physics-guided workflow connecting characterization, screening, descriptor families, concentration, response models, and physical checks. Physics-guided descriptor framework · Schematic View full image → Characterization Extract structural, chemical, vibrational, porosity, and dispersion information. Descriptor construction Screen variables and construct explicit, interpretable material coordinates. Response modelling Compare compact relationships with concentration and selected material descriptors. Regression parameters remain estimated from observations. Physics supplies constraints and interpretation; this is not a first-principles calculation of optical absorption. Before the fit Screen the information entering the model. Check Question Why it matters Comparability Are the measured features physically equivalent? Prevents unrelated peaks or measurement definitions from being compared. Completeness Are inputs available and quantifiable? Missing and below-threshold values require explicit treatment rather than automatic zeros. Acquisition sensitivity Could instrument settings dominate the quantity? Limits reliance on uncontrolled absolute intensity. Redundancy Do variables repeat the same information? Reduces duplicated influence and unstable predictor combinations. Assumption dependence Is the quantity measured or model-derived? Separates independent inputs from assumed-parameter outputs. Circularity Was the variable derived from the response? Avoids reusing response information as an independent predictor. Descriptor screening table; scroll horizontally on small screens Material coordinates Three descriptor families, with explicit definitions. Normalize before combining Selected inputs are placed on a common scale. Feature direction and weighting are documented as part of the score definition. N(x) = (x − xmin) / (xmax − xmin) Ninverse(x) = 1 − N(x) Constant-valued features require exclusion or separately defined treatment. I Structure & interface Combines apparent stacking coherence, FTIR B2 band-area fraction, F/Ti, and pore diameter. I = [1 − N(Lc) + N(B2 fraction) + N(F/Ti) + N(Dp)] / 4 The inverted direction for Lc is an explicit choice in this score definition. D Vibrational features Retains a selected corresponding Raman-shift variable as a vibrational-change coordinate. D = N(selected Raman-shift variable) Distinct from linewidth-based broadening and a universal measure of disorder. S Dispersion Combines electrokinetic magnitude and operational hydrodynamic size. S = [1 − N(log10Dh) + N(|ζ|)] / 2 DLS size can include aggregates; it is not a direct sheet-width measure. These equal-weight scores are comparative within the defined material set, rather than universal constants. Defining I, D, and S does not require fitting all three together or establish a universal direction of performance. Explore the individual characterization descriptors → Response modelling Separate concentration from material information. Concentration describes an experimental condition. Material scores summarize characterization. Reduced candidate models keep those roles explicit. Qnet = β0 + βC ln(C/C0) + βSS Purpose: represent concentration dependence alongside a selected material descriptor. C0 is a reference concentration that makes the logarithm dimensionless. No fitted coefficients are displayed here. Compare candidate response shapes Linear, logarithmic, power-law, and saturation forms express different concentration dependencies. Physical motivation guides the candidates; model checks assess their support. Q(C) = QmaxC / (KC + C) This saturation candidate permits diminishing increments. A fit alone does not establish an optical or aggregation mechanism. Retain the energy balance Thermal storage, input, and loss define the physical meaning of the response target. Measured, fitted, and extrapolated quantities remain distinct. Csys dΔT/dt = Qin − HΔT ΔT∞ = Qin/H The equilibrium relation assumes constant effective input. A finite-time switch-off estimator is not silently substituted for equilibrium heat input. Assess the relationship Examine sensitivity, stability, and scope. Descriptor choices affect the relationship. Assessment examines alternative definitions, residual structure, parameter stability, and uncertainty alongside model complexity. Assessment Purpose Descriptor alternatives Compare FTIR fractions with ratios, pore measures, and linear versus logarithmic size transforms. Residual inspection Identify systematic behaviour the candidate model does not capture. Parameter stability Examine dependence on individual observations and correlated predictors. Complexity Limit adjustable terms to what the available material set can support. Uncertainty Track contributions from transient fitting, reference calibration, and descriptor construction. Validation scope Distinguish interpolation within measured conditions from prediction for new materials. Model assessment table; scroll horizontally on small screens Multiple concentrations of one material do not create multiple independent material descriptors. The number of distinct characterized materials limits material-level generalization. Withheld-data checks must reflect the prediction task being assessed. MATLAB implementation A traceable path from measurements to models. Assemble the input table Preserve material identity, measurement origin, units, and missing-value status. Screen candidate variables Check comparability, redundancy, acquisition sensitivity, and assumptions. Define the scores Document normalization ranges, transformations, feature directions, and weights. Specify the response target Keep switch-off estimators, asymptotic quantities, and direct temperature measurements distinct. Fit reduced candidate models Compare concentration functions and selected descriptor terms with controlled complexity. Assess the relationship Examine residuals, sensitivity, uncertainty, physical consistency, and validation scope. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Alternative fuels / Plastic fuel Plastic-Derived Fuels My work investigates the conversion of waste plastics into liquid fuels through pyrolysis. These photographs document the equipment, liquid product collection, and samples used in this research. Overview Biodiesel Plastic Fuel Combustion and Emission Nanoparticles Alternative fuels research Research Overview Pyrolysis breaks down plastics through heating in an oxygen-limited environment. The resulting vapours can be cooled and collected as liquid products. My research explores plastic-derived fuels within the broader study of alternative fuels, engine performance, combustion, and emissions. entries.text: Skip to content Home / Research Research Interests My research focuses on understanding the relationships between material processing, structure, surface chemistry, and functional performance. My work integrates experimental characterization, quantitative analysis, and physics-guided modelling, with applications in sustainable energy, functional materials, and engineering. Research interests Publications Conferences Research sections 01 / TWO-DIMENSIONAL MATERIALS MXenes & Functional Composites Synthesis, processing, and characterization of titanium-based MXenes, including selective etching, DMSO intercalation, and transition-metal sulfide composites. Investigation of processing-induced changes in structure, surface chemistry, morphology, and elemental composition. MXenes XRD Raman XPS Methods and topics Explore materials → 02 / FUNCTIONAL MATERIAL STUDIES Photothermal & Electrochemical Studies Experimental investigations of laser-induced heating and electrochemical behaviour in functional materials. Explore two study areas covering temperature evolution, heat generation, electrode activity, charge transfer, and reaction kinetics. Photothermal Electrochemistry MXenes Methods and topics Choose a study area → 03 / MODELLING AND DESCRIPTORS Modelling & Descriptor Development Development of MATLAB models and physics-guided descriptors to investigate relationships between material properties and measured behaviour. Model formulation, physical interpretation, and comparison with experimental measurements provide the basis for evaluating these relationships. MATLAB Physical Models Descriptors Validation Methods and topics Explore modelling → 04 / MAGNETIC MATERIALS Complex Magnetic Oxides Structural and magnetic investigations of complex oxide materials using X-ray diffraction, Rietveld refinement, Raman spectroscopy, and magnetic measurements. Exploration of relationships between crystal structure and magnetic behaviour. Magnetism Rietveld Raman PPMS Methods and topics Explore magnetic materials → 05 / SUSTAINABLE ENERGY Alternative Fuels & Nanoparticles Experimental investigations of biodiesel, waste plastic pyrolysis oil, and nanoparticle-enhanced fuel blends. Evaluation of combustion characteristics, engine performance, and emissions in internal combustion engines. Biodiesel Plastic Fuel Combustion and Emission Nanoparticles Methods and topics Explore fuel research → 06 / QUANTITATIVE ANALYSIS Scientific Data Analysis Computational processing and interpretation of experimental measurements using MATLAB, spectral fitting, statistical methods, and kinetic analysis. Comparison of experimental datasets, interpretation of fitted parameters, and clear visualization of scientific measurements. MATLAB Spectral Fitting Statistics Methods and topics Explore data analysis → Six research areas Rupesh Lal Karn Prairie View, Texas rkarn@pvamu.edu Google Scholar ORCID CV Projects Contact Academic profiles © 2026 Rupesh Lal Karn
