entries.title: Thermal Kinetics & TGA Simulation
entries.description: Explore multi-rate TGA and DTG analysis, Kissinger and isoconversional kinetics, activation-energy extraction, and MATLAB simulation of thermal events.
entries.headings: Thermal Kinetics & TGA Simulation Start with mass loss and its rate. Express mass loss as conversion. Five techniques, two comparison strategies. Kissinger FWO KAS Starink Friedman From activation energy to a simulated event. The modelling sequence, step by step. Quantities carried into interpretation
entries.text: Skip to content Research / Modelling / TGA Thermal Kinetics & TGA Simulation I use multi-rate thermogravimetric measurements to identify thermal events, extract apparent activation energies, and reconstruct event-specific mass-loss behaviour. The framework combines DTG peak analysis, isoconversional methods, and numerical integration for MAX, acid-etched MXene, and DMSO-treated MXene. TGA & DTG Conversion Kinetic techniques Simulation Major steps Page sections Schematic multi-rate TGA curves and corresponding DTG peak shifts. Multi-rate TGA · Schematic Enlarge Identify the thermal event Start with mass loss and its rate. TGA measures remaining mass as temperature increases. DTG highlights where mass loss occurs most rapidly, helping locate event boundaries and peak temperatures. Measurements at different heating rates allow the same event to be compared across temperature shifts. Corresponding events must be identified before estimating kinetic parameters. Derivative thermogravimetry DTG = −dm / dT With this sign convention, mass-loss events appear as positive peaks. Tp is the temperature of the selected DTG maximum. Normalize the selected event Express mass loss as conversion. Each selected thermal event receives its own initial and final mass references. Conversion then describes progress through that event rather than through the entire thermogram. Event-specific conversion α(T) = [m0 − m(T)] / [m0 − mf] α = 0 at the event start and α = 1 at its selected end. m0 and mf refer to that event’s boundaries. Non-isothermal kinetic equation dα/dT = (A/β) exp[−Ea/(RT)] f(α) β = dT/dt The Arrhenius term describes temperature dependence. f(α) represents the assumed conversion dependence. α Event-specific conversion β Heating rate, dT/dt T Absolute temperature in kelvin Ea Apparent activation energy A Apparent pre-exponential factor R Gas constant Compare kinetic descriptions Five techniques, two comparison strategies. Kissinger tracks the DTG peak. FWO, KAS, Starink, and Friedman compare measurements at a fixed conversion α, using the temperature Tα reached at each heating rate. Schematic regression plots for Kissinger, FWO, KAS, Starink, and Friedman methods. Kinetic techniques · Schematic Enlarge Kissinger DTG peak-based analysis Tracks how the selected peak temperature changes with heating rate. Provides an apparent event-level activation-energy estimate. ln(β/Tp2) = C − Ea/(RTp) Plot: ln(β/Tp2) against 1/Tp. From slope s: Ea = −Rs. FWO Flynn–Wall–Ozawa · Integral isoconversional Compares heating rates at the same conversion without selecting a reaction-order function. Repeating the calculation across α gives an apparent activation-energy profile. log10β = Cα − 0.4567 Ea,α/(RTα) Plot: log10β against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs/0.4567. KAS Kissinger–Akahira–Sunose · Integral isoconversional Uses a temperature-corrected heating-rate transformation at fixed conversion. Complements FWO through a different integral approximation. ln(β/Tα2) = Cα − Ea,α/(RTα) Plot: ln(β/Tα2) against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs. Starink Integral isoconversional Applies an alternative temperature-integral approximation. Provides another comparison of conversion-dependent apparent activation energies. ln(β/Tα1.92) = Cα − 1.0008 Ea,α/(RTα) Plot: ln(β/Tα1.92) against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs/1.0008. Friedman Differential isoconversional Uses the conversion rate directly at fixed α. Supplies a differential comparison with the integral methods and requires careful derivative treatment. ln(dα/dt) = ln[A f(α)] − Ea,α/(RTα) dα/dt = β(dα/dT) Plot: ln(dα/dt) against 1/Tα. From slope: Ea,α = −Rs. C and Cα denote intercept terms. Temperature is expressed in kelvin and heating-rate units remain consistent. These methods estimate apparent kinetic quantities; agreement does not establish a unique mechanism. Reconstruct the measured event From activation energy to a simulated event. For event reconstruction, selected apparent activation-energy descriptors enter an effective first-order kinetic equation. The order is fixed at n = 1, while A is fitted separately for each experimental heating rate. General apparent event model dα/dT = (A/β) exp[−Ea/(RT)] (1 − α)n Effective first-order reconstruction: n = 1 dα/dT = (A/β) exp[−Ea/(RT)](1 − α) Numerically integrate over the selected temperature interval using the event boundary as the initial condition. Convert simulated conversion back to mass msim(T) = m0 − αsim(T)(m0 − mf) This reconstructs the mass change within the selected event. Multiple-event models require separately defined event contributions and mass-loss weights. Because A is fitted separately at each heating rate, this is an event-reconstruction test. It does not by itself demonstrate prediction at an unseen heating rate. The first-order form is an effective representation, rather than proof of first-order reaction chemistry. MATLAB workflow The modelling sequence, step by step. Import the multi-rate measurements Preserve mass, temperature, heating rate, sample identity, and acquisition conditions. Convert temperature to kelvin for kinetic calculations. Process the thermograms and calculate DTG Check the mass baseline and derivative sensitivity. Identify peak temperatures and candidate event boundaries. Match corresponding events Compare compatible transformations across heating rates. Screen events with unresolved overlap or inconsistent boundaries. Calculate event-specific conversion Normalize each event using its boundary masses. Interpolate Tα and conversion rates on a common conversion grid. Apply the five kinetic methods Use DTG peak temperatures for Kissinger. Use matched conversion levels for FWO, KAS, Starink, and Friedman. Assess the kinetic descriptors Examine regression quality, conversion-window stability, derivative sensitivity, and agreement between methods. Retain event-level descriptors only after screening. Integrate the event model Use the selected apparent activation energy, fix n = 1, and fit A for each heating rate. Reconstruct conversion and then mass. Inspect reconstruction quality Compare simulated and measured conversion profiles, inspect residuals, and assess systematic deviations. Retain the model assumptions alongside the descriptors. Quantities carried into interpretation Event mass fraction Mass lost within the selected interval, reported with its normalization basis. Onset & offset temperatures Operational boundaries used to define and compare the thermal event. DTG peak temperature Temperature of the maximum mass-loss rate under the stated sign convention. Ea versus conversion Apparent activation-energy profile obtained at matched conversion levels. Event-level apparent Ea Selected energy descriptor retained after method and conversion-window screening. Fitted apparent A Rate-specific pre-exponential factor used in the effective reconstruction model. Reconstruction diagnostics Residuals and profile agreement used to assess the selected event model. These quantities describe thermal events at different levels of detail. They are kept distinct from unique mechanistic constants or a single kinetic description of the entire thermogram. ← Back to modelling Characterization descriptors → Rupesh Lal Karn Prairie View, Texas rkarn@pvamu.edu Google Scholar ORCID CV Projects Contact Academic profiles © 2026 Rupesh Lal Karn

entries.text: Skip to content Engineering projects / TRICAR Undergraduate engineering project · Team-built prototype TRICAR From a digital chassis model to a fabricated three-wheeled vehicle. This project brought together mechanical design, workshop fabrication, component integration, and collaborative assembly. CAD modelling · Chassis fabrication · Steering integration · Vehicle assembly Side view of the TRICAR prototype with its exposed tubular frame, blue seat, and seated driver. View original TRICAR cover photograph The assembled TRICAR prototype View original → Project background Design, Fabrication & Assembly TRICAR is a mechanical engineering project involving the design, simulation, fabrication, and assembly of a three-wheeled vehicle. Working as part of the project team, I contributed to bringing the vehicle concept into a physical prototype. The photographs document the tubular chassis, steering arrangement, workshop fabrication, mechanical assembly, and team activities. The CAD model provides a view of the overall vehicle layout before and alongside fabrication. Vehicle layout and CAD Development of the chassis concept and component layout, considering the driver’s seating position, wheel arrangement, and available space for mechanical systems. Building the chassis Workshop fabrication and joining of tubular frame members to turn the vehicle layout into a physical structure. Mechanical integration Integration of steering, wheels, seating, and other mechanical components through collaborative assembly work. From Design to Assembly Seven images document the CAD layout, chassis fabrication, component integration, and team activities. Select an image to view the original in this tab. entries.text: Skip to content Research / Two-dimensional materials MXenes & Functional Composites I study Ti₃AlCN-derived Ti₃CNTₓ MXenes and transition-metal sulfide composites, examining how processing changes their structure, surface chemistry, morphology, and functional response. My work combines synthesis and intercalation with complementary characterization, photothermal and electrochemical measurements, and physics-guided descriptor analysis. My Primary MXene System Ti₃CNTₓ Layered titanium carbonitride MXene Tₓ denotes surface terminations introduced or modified during processing. About MXenes Processing Research questions Composites Characterization Functional studies Page sections The material family A layered framework with chemically active surfaces. MXenes are a family of two-dimensional transition-metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides. Their metal–carbon or metal–nitrogen framework is combined with surface groups that interact with surrounding molecules, ions, and other material phases. The family is studied for electrical conductivity, accessible surfaces, and tunable interlayer chemistry. In practice, performance depends on how the sheets are prepared, stacked, dispersed, and combined with other materials. Mn+1XnTx M An early transition metal; titanium in my primary material system. X Carbon and/or nitrogen within the layered framework. Tx Surface terminations, which can include oxygen-, hydroxyl-, and fluorine-containing groups depending on the preparation route. Material preparation Track the material through each processing state. I compare the precursor and processed MXene states so that structural, chemical, and functional measurements retain a clear preparation history. Ti₃AlCN MAX precursor The layered precursor supplies the starting structure and a reference for examining selective aluminium removal and subsequent material changes. Acid-etched MXene LiF/HCl etching is followed by centrifugation and washing to remove residual acid and soluble by-products. The recovered material is examined for changes in phase signatures, stacking, and surface chemistry. DMSO-treated MXene DMSO treatment promotes intercalation between layers. Washing and recovery prepare the treated material for comparisons of layer arrangement, dispersion, and measured response. Processing–structure relationships What changes when the layers are modified? Interlayer arrangement How do etching and intercalation affect basal spacing, stacking coherence, and the arrangement of layered assemblies? I use diffraction alongside complementary measurements to examine these questions. Surface chemistry How do surface composition and selected chemical environments change with treatment? Spectroscopic analysis helps distinguish surface-related contributions from changes in the underlying material framework. Dispersion & restacking How do the processed sheets assemble in suspension? Zeta potential, DLS, morphology, and gas-sorption measurements provide complementary information on dispersion and accessible interfaces. Structure & functional response Which measured structural and interfacial variables are useful for interpreting thermal stability, irradiation-induced heating, and electrochemical behaviour? Descriptor-based analysis connects these measurements while retaining their assumptions. MXene–sulfide systems A layered host with additional interfaces. My work also includes MXene-based composite systems containing transition-metal sulfides. These systems extend the research from modifying a layered material to examining how secondary phases are distributed and connected with it. NiS₂ CuS₂ ZnS MoS₂ Sulfide systems The questions include phase identification, morphology, elemental distribution, and surface-chemical changes associated with composite preparation. The aim is to understand the interfaces rather than assume that combining materials automatically improves performance. Composite interpretation draws on XRD, Raman, FTIR, XPS, and SEM/EDS. Structural and spatial evidence are considered together when examining the relationship between constituent phases. Complementary measurements Build the material picture from several measurements. Each technique probes a different part of the system. I combine their information to examine structure, chemistry, accessible interfaces, dispersion, and stability. Method What I examine Connection to the research XRD Phase signatures, basal reflections, peak positions, and broadening Layer spacing, stacking, and processing-dependent structural changes Raman & FTIR Vibrational features, peak shifts, linewidths, and selected band areas Comparative information on the framework, surface groups, and interfacial environments XPS Near-surface composition and fitted chemical-envelope contributions Surface-chemical changes associated with etching, treatment, and composite preparation SEM / EDS Morphology and elemental distribution Layered assemblies, aggregates, and spatial context for constituent phases BET / gas sorption Gas-accessible area, pore volume, and operational pore descriptors Accessible interfaces and pore-related material coordinates Zeta potential & DLS Electrokinetic response and hydrodynamic size Operational comparisons of dispersion under defined measurement conditions TGA / DTG Mass-loss events, conversion, and heating-rate dependence Thermal stability, apparent kinetics, and event-specific reconstruction Optical measurements Optical-response features considered with other characterization Context for interpreting irradiation-induced heating MXene characterization methods; scroll horizontally on small screens Explore characterization-derived descriptors → From materials to response Connect preparation with measured performance. Photothermal studies Near-infrared heating–cooling measurements examine how processing state and suspension concentration relate to the temperature response. entries.text: Skip to content Home/ Projects/ Undergraduate research Breadcrumb Thapathali Campus · Undergraduate project · 2019 Testing of Performance and Emission Characteristics of Plastic Pyrolysis Oil and Jatropha Blend in IC Engines From fuel preparation to the engine test bench. A team investigation of diesel blends containing either plastic-derived oil or Jatropha biodiesel, connecting fuel properties with engine performance and smoke opacity. Explore the experimental work ↓ Institution Thapathali Campus Institute of Engineering, Tribhuvan University Programme Bachelor in Automobile Engineering Kathmandu, Nepal My role Undergraduate project team member Report submitted 11 August 2019 Study summary Abstract Adapted from the 2019 undergraduate project report for web presentation. An experimental investigation evaluated Jatropha biodiesel–diesel blends and Plasto diesel blends (PDB) through fuel-property measurements, engine-performance testing, and smoke-opacity assessment. Thermophysical properties were examined for JB20, containing 20% Jatropha biodiesel by volume, and PDB10, containing 10% plastic-derived fuel by volume. Engine tests covered Jatropha blends up to 20% and Plasto diesel blends up to 15%, with diesel as the reference fuel. The study compared indicated and brake power, thermal efficiency, specific fuel consumption, and fuel-consumption rate. The report found relatively small differences in brake power among the tested fuels and identified JB20 and PDB15 as promising blends within the evaluated performance measures. All tested blends were reported to pass the smoke-opacity test. Under the investigated conditions, the report described favourable performance of Plasto diesel blends relative to Jatropha blends. These findings apply to the blend fractions, equipment, and operating conditions evaluated in the project. The emissions comparison was limited to smoke opacity; NOₓ, SOₓ, HC, and CO were not measured. Experimental design Two fuel families. A diesel reference. Jatropha biodiesel + diesel JB5 · JB10 · JB15 · JB20 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% Jatropha biodiesel by volume; diesel makes up the remainder. Plasto diesel blend (PDB) PDB5 · PDB10 · PDB15 PDB means Plasto diesel blend. PDB5, PDB10, and PDB15 contain 5%, 10%, and 15% plastic-derived fuel by volume, respectively; diesel makes up the remainder. The reported engine comparisons treat these as separate blend series, each tested against diesel. Experimental workflow Preparation, measurement, comparison. Prepare the fuels Plastic processing involved batch-reactor pyrolysis, filtration, and fractional distillation. The Jatropha pathway used transesterified oil for biodiesel blends. Characterize the samples Fuel-property evaluation included density, viscosity, flash and pour points, calorific value, and cetane assessment. FTIR supported comparison of chemical signatures. Test against diesel Compare blend behaviour under engine loading, recording performance and fuel-consumption measures. Smoke testing provided a separate exhaust-opacity assessment. Interpret the response Examine how power, efficiency, fuel use, and opacity vary with blend fraction and test conditions, alongside the measured fuel properties. Test bench & analysis What Was Evaluated The performance-test setup was a single-cylinder, four-stroke, constant-speed, water-cooled diesel engine, rated at 3.50 kW at 1500 rpm, with a compression ratio of 18:1. Power & torque Indicated power, brake power, and torque as functions of engine load. Efficiency Indicated and brake thermal efficiency, mechanical efficiency, and volumetric efficiency. Fuel consumption Fuel-consumption rate and specific fuel consumption for the blend series and diesel reference. Smoke opacity Exhaust-smoke assessment using an RTM 430 opacimeter. Emissions measurement scope The project assessed smoke opacity. NOₓ, SOₓ, HC, and CO were not measured because a five-gas analyser was unavailable during the study. entries.text: Processing-Induced Structural and Surface-Chemical Evolution in Ti₃AlCN-Derived Ti₃CNTₓ Rupesh Lal Karn1, Gururaj M Neelgund2*, Raghava R. Kommalapati3* 1Department of Mechanical Engineering 3Department of Chemistry and Physics 2Center for Energy and Environmental Sustainability Prairie View A&M University, Prairie View, TX 77446 rkarn@pvamu.edu, rrkommalapati@pvamu.edu, GMNeelgund@PVAMU.EDU Abstract The properties of MXenes are strongly dependent on processing-induced changes in their surface and structure. Herein, MAX phase Ti₃AlCN has been modified into Ti₃CNTₓ by the treatment of LiF/HCl followed by dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Thus produced Ti₃CNTₓ was characterized using different techniques. The photothermal effect of Ti₃CNTₓ has been determined at different concentrations by illuminating to 980 nm NIR laser. The XRD of Ti₃CNTₓ revealed its basal expansion, with 𝑑002 increasing from 9.13 Å (MAX) to 13.77 Å (acid-etched) and 14.23 Å (DMSO-treated). The XPS confirmed the removal of Al by etching and the development of an oxide-dominated Ti surface. The Raman analysis showed the progressive modification of the parent lattice. The photothermal effect of acid-etched Ti₃CNTₓ raised the temperature to 59.26°C after 7 min of laser illumination to the laser having a power density of 1 W. The photothermal effect of acid-etched Ti₃CNTₓ was higher than DMSO treated Ti₃CNTₓ. It revealed that interlayer expansion in DMSO treated Ti₃CNTₓ Figure 4: BET-derived textural and transport descriptors for MAX, acid-etched, and DMSO-treated does not improve the photothermal effect, which could be due to coupled roles MXene, showing changes in surface area, pore volume, porosity, surface-area density, interface factor, of structure, surface chemistry, and vibrational state. and predicted effective conductivity. Method and descriptor extraction Figure 7: Experimental and modeled photothermal heating–cooling profiles of MAX, acid-etched, and DMSO-treated MXene at 1, 2, and 4 mg/mL, showing concentration-dependent temperature rise and excellent agreement between experiment and fitted thermal- response models. Figure 1: Processing pathway from Ti₃AlCN MAX to acid-etched and DMSO-treated Ti₃CNTₓ MXene, illustrating Al removal, surface termination, and interlayer expansion Figure 5: . FTIR-based descriptor extraction for MAX, acid-etched, and DMSO-treated MXene, showing characteristic band regions, transmittance-depth changes, and comparative surface-, defect-, and OH/interface-related spectral descriptors. Mailing Address : Rupesh Lal Karn P.O Box: 232 Prairie View, TX 77446 Mobile No. : +1832-803-7501, E-mail : rkarn@pvamu.edu , karnrupesh300@gmail.com rupeshkarn@tcioe.edu.np ORCID : 0009-0008-9261-024X PERSONAL PROFILE STATEMENT I am an interdisciplinary materials researcher with 14 peer-reviewed publications and research experience at two U.S. national laboratories. My background spans applied nanoparticle systems, Mn-based magnetic oxides, single-crystal materials, MXene-based 2D materials, and metal sulfide nanocomposites. My current research combines nanomaterial synthesis, advanced characterization, electrochemical analysis, MATLAB-supported modeling, and descriptor-based interpretation of experimental data to study structure–property relationships in functional materials. I have experience with XRD, Rietveld refinement, Raman spectroscopy, XPS, SEM/EDX, BET, TGA/DSC, Lorentz TEM data analysis, electrochemical measurements, thermal/photothermal simulation, TGA kinetic modeling, and physics-based data analysis. My broader interest is in connecting layered-material structure, surface chemistry, interlayer modification, charge-transfer behavior, thermal stability, and interfaces with measurable performance in MXene-based and energy-related material systems. RESEARCH INTEREST My research interest focuses on MXenes, layered materials, and nanostructured functional materials for electrochemical energy applications. I am especially interested in using synthesis, characterization, and physics- based modeling to understand ion interaction, charge-storage behavior, phase evolution, and performance- controlling mechanisms in nanoscale material systems. My long-term goal is to develop descriptor-driven structure–property frameworks that can guide the design of MXene-based materials, transition-metal compounds, and related materials for energy storage, electrocatalysis, and other electrochemical technologies.
